rationale: A wins because it finds one more real newsroom shape without turning it into confetti: “The AI agent's biggest savings didn't come from negotiating. They came from cancelling.” is a useful contrarian lens, even if the word “cancelling” needs tightening. B is strong, but “AI agents are moving into real finance work” is the safer, duller version of A's governance angle, and it leaves the more interesting anti-hype interpretation on the table. Both sets understand that $342,000 is the story only if the methodology survives daylight.
gaps_in_A: “The AI agent's biggest savings didn't come from negotiating. They came from cancelling.” overstates the supplied facts. The update says savings were mostly from unused seats and auto-renewals, not that cancellations beat renegotiations in realized dollars.
“plans to charge enterprises later” is an inference from “enterprise tier,” not a stated fact. Reasonable, but it should be framed as likely monetization, not confirmed pricing strategy.

The vendor-conflict angle says the tool “attacks revenue lines vendors have quietly relied on.” Good line, but it needs care: the update gives unused seats and auto-renewals, not evidence of vendor intent or reliance.
gaps_in_B: It misses the strongest contrarian angle: the beta suggests agent value may come from boring software hygiene, not glamorous negotiation. That is a real column-shaped story, and B walks past it.
“AI agents are moving into real finance work” is competent but broad. It starts sounding like the thousandth enterprise-AI trend piece until the approval workflow details rescue it.
“with a measured outcome ($342K average) attached” is a little too clean. The update says savings were found in beta; it does not prove the money was actually banked.
The refused angle “How one company clawed back $342,000 in dead SaaS seats” is labeled only as `duplicate`, but the bigger offense is fabrication: no named company and no confirmed clawback.
